COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Overview
❑ What is a cluster?  
▪ A cluster is a collection of data objects
• Objects are similar (or related) to one another within the same group 
• Objects are dissimilar (or unrelated) to the objects in other groups
▪ Examples

COSE471: Data Science

Clustering > Overview
❑ Cluster analysis (or clustering, data segmentation, …)
▪ Given a set of data points, partition them into a set of groups (i.e., clusters)
▪ Learning philosophy
• Unsupervised learning with unknown cluster labels
• cf. classification is supervised learning with known class labels

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Overview
❑ Cluster analysis (or clustering, data segmentation, …)
▪ Given a set of data points, partition them into a set of groups (i.e., clusters)
▪ Learning philosophy
• Unsupervised learning with unknown cluster labels
• cf. classification is supervised learning with known class labels
▪ Quality
• A good clustering method will produce high-quality clusters
‒ High intra-class similarity → cohesive within clusters
‒ Low inter-class similarity → distinctive between clusters
• There are usually separate quality measures for the “goodness” of a cluster for different applications
‒ It is hard to define “similar enough” or “good enough” → The answer is typically highly subjective
8

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Applications 
❑ A stand-alone tool to get insight into data distribution
▪ Visual insights - one picture is worth a thousand words
❑ A key intermediate step for other data science tasks
▪ A compact summary of data for downstream tasks
• e.g., the basis for classification, pattern discovery, outlier detection
▪ Data summarization, compression, and reduction
• e.g. binning, discretization, sampling
▪ Recommendation systems, customer segmentation
• e.g. Finding like-minded users or similar products
▪ Multimedia data, biological data, and social data analysis
• e.g.. grouping images/video/audio, gene/protein sequences, trend detection and tracking
11
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Considerations 
❑ Partitioning criteria
▪ Single level vs. hierarchical partitioning
▪ e.g., flat concepts (gender) vs. multi-level concepts (county – city – country – continent) 
❑ Cluster separation
▪ Exclusive vs. non-exclusive
▪ e.g., a customer belongs to only one region vs. a news article may belong to multiple topics
❑ Similarity measure
▪ Distance-based vs. connectivity-based
▪ e.g., Euclidean, road network, vector vs. density or contiguity
❑ Clustering space
▪ Full space vs. subspaces
▪ e.g., Low dimensional vs. high-dimensional
12

▪ Distance-based
▪ Density-based

▪ High-dimensional

❑ Data type
▪ Numerical data, categorical data, text data, multimedia data, time-series data, sequence data, 
streaming data, network data
❑ Additional insight
▪ Visual insights, semi-supervised, ensemble-based, validation-based

Clustering > Distance-based > Partitioning
❑ Partitioning method
▪ Discovering the groupings in a dataset based on the distances of data objects
▪ Problem definition
• Given k, find a partition of k clusters that optimizes the chosen distance-based objective function 
• e.g., minimize the sum of squared errors between objects and centers in clusters, σ𝐶𝑘∈𝐶 σ𝑥𝑖 ∈𝐶𝑘 𝑑(𝑥𝑖, 𝑐𝑘)2

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Distance-based > Partitioning
❑ Partitioning method
▪ Discovering the groupings in a dataset based on the distances of data objects
▪ Problem definition
• Given k, find a partition of k clusters that optimizes the chosen distance-based objective function 
• e.g., minimize the sum of squared errors between objects and centers in clusters, σ𝐶𝑘∈𝐶 σ𝑥𝑖 ∈𝐶𝑘 𝑑(𝑥𝑖, 𝑐𝑘)2
▪ Approaches
• Global optimal needs to exhaustively enumerate all possible partitions
• Heuristic methods (i.e., greedy algorithms): k-Means, k-Medoids, k-Medians, etc.

❑ k-Means clustering
▪ Each cluster is represented by the cluster center and the sum of d(object, center) 2 is minimized
• i.e., minimize the sum of squared errors (SSE) in clusters

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Distance-based > Partitioning > k-Means
❑ k-Means clustering
▪ Each cluster is represented by the cluster center and the sum of d(object, center)2 is minimized
❑ Procedures with a given number of clusters k
▪ Select k objects as initial centroids (centers)
▪ Repeat
• Form k clusters by assigning each object to its closest centroid
• Re-compute the centroids of each cluster
‒ i.e., the average value of objects in each cluster 
▪ Until the convergence criterion is satisfied 
• e.g., the centroids do not change
❑ Interactive demo
19

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Distance-based > Partitioning > k-Means
❑ Complexity: O(tkn)
▪ n: # of objects, k: # of clusters, t: # of iterations (usually, k, t << n)
❑ Limitations
▪ Applicable only to objects in a continuous space 
▪ Need to specify k, the number of clusters, in advance
▪ Often terminates at a local optimal
▪ Sensitive to noisy data and outliers
▪ Not suitable to discover clusters with non-convex shapes or 
clusters of very different sizes or density
❑ Variants
▪ Better initial centroid estimates (e.g., k-means++)
▪ Different representative cluster prototypes (e.g., k-Medoids)
▪ Feature transformation (e.g., Kernel method or embedding)
22

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Distance-based > Partitioning > k-Means++
❑ k-Means++ clustering
▪ Pick the initial centroids sequentially with a weighted probability score and conduct k-Means
❑ Procedures with a given number clusters k
▪ Select an initial object at random to be the first centroid
▪ For k – 1 steps
• For remaining objects, find the squared distance 𝑚𝑖𝑛𝑗 𝑑(𝑥𝑖, 𝑐𝑗)2 to the nearest centroid
• Randomly select a new centroid by choosing an object with probability proportional to
‒ i.e., further from existing centroids, higher probability to be picked
▪ End For
▪ Conduct standard k-Means clustering with the initial centroids

Clustering > Distance-based > Partitioning > k-Medoids
❑ k-Medoids clustering (better cluster prototypes)
▪ Each cluster is represented by the cluster medoid and the sum of d(object, medoid)2 is minimized
• Medoids: the most centrally located object in a cluster
▪ More robust to outliers than k-Means

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Distance-based > Partitioning > k-Medoids
❑ k-Medoids clustering
▪ Each cluster is represented by the cluster medoid and the sum of d(object, medoid)2 is minimized
• Medoid: the most centrally located object in a cluster
▪ Procedures of PAM (Partitioning Around Medoids)
• Select k points as the initial medoids
• Repeat
‒ Assigning each point to the cluster with the closest medoid 
‒ Get the total cost (e.g., SSE) of swapping the medoid with a non-medoid
‒ If the total cost decreases, swap the medoid with the chosen object 
• Until convergence criterion is satisfied
▪ Issue
• Not scalable with large data due to high computational complexity
• i.e., O(tk(n-k)2) > O(tkn) where t is the number of iterations
29

COSE471: Data Science

Clustering > Distance-based > Hierarchical
❑ Hierarchical clustering  
▪ Generate a clustering hierarchy, visualized as a dendrogram
▪ Not required to specify the number of clusters (k)
• The desired number of clusters can be obtained by cutting the dendrogram at the proper level
▪ More deterministic than partitioning approaches
• No iterative refinement required

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Distance-based > Hierarchical
❑ Two approaches
▪ Agglomerative (i.e., bottom-up)
• Start with the points as individual clusters
• Merge the closest pair of clusters continuously
▪ Divisive (i.e., top-down)
• Start with one, all-inclusive cluster
• Split it continuously into two clusters
34

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Distance-based > Hierarchical
❑ Cluster distance measures for split/merge
▪ Single link (min)
• Smallest distance between an object in one cluster and an object in the other
• i.e., d(Ci, Cj) = min(d(xip, xjq))
▪ Complete link (max)
• Largest distance between an object in one cluster and an object in the other 
• i.e., d(Ci, Cj) = max(d(xip, xjq))
▪ Average link
• Average distance between an object in one cluster and an object in the other 
• i.e., d(Ci, Cj) = avg(d(xip, xjq))
▪ Centroid link
• Distance between the centroids of two clusters
• i.e., d(Ci, Cj) = d(ci, cj)
▪ Ward link
• The change in the SSE of the clusters (i.e., similar to the partitioning approach)
• i.e., ∆d(Ci, Cj) =σ𝑥𝑘∈𝐶𝑖∪𝐶𝑗 d(𝑥𝑘,𝑐𝑛𝑒𝑤)2 − (σ𝑥𝑘∈𝐶𝑖 d(𝑥𝑘,𝑐𝑖)2 + σ𝑥𝑘∈𝐶𝑗 d(𝑥𝑘,𝑐𝑗)2) =
𝑁𝑖𝑁𝑗
𝑁𝑖+𝑁𝑗
d(𝑐𝑖,𝑐𝑗)2

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Distance-based > Hierarchical > BIRCH
❑ Limitation of Hierarchical Approach
▪ Not reversible merge and split at each level
▪ Not scalable with the time complexity O(n3) (i.e., pairwise distances O(n2) for up to n-1 levels)
❑ Efficient multi-phase hierarchical clustering
▪ Challenge: calculating various distance statistics repeatedly?
• Basis distance measures
‒ Centroid (average of objects) 
‒ Radius (average distance to centroid) 
‒ Diameter (average pair-wise distance) 
• Additional distance measures
‒ D0 = Euclidean distance of two clusters
‒ D1 = Manhattan distance of two clusters
‒ D2 = Average inter-cluster distance
‒ D3 = Average intra-cluster distance
‒ D4 = Variance increase distance

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Distance-based > Hierarchical > BIRCH
❑ BIRCH (Balanced Iterative Reducing and Clustering Using Hierarchies)
▪ Clustering feature (CF) to summarize a cluster and CF-tree to represent a cluster hierarchy
• Clustering feature CF = (N, LS, SS)
‒ N: Number of data points 
‒ LS: linear sum of N points: σ𝑖=1
𝑁 𝑋𝑖
‒ SS: square sum of N points:σ𝑖=1
𝑁 𝑋𝑖
2
• CF-tree
‒ A height-balanced tree that stores the CFs of clusters (nodes)
‒ The non-leaf nodes store the sum of CFs of their child nodes

C1 = {(3,4), (2,6), (4,5), (4,7), (3,8)}

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Distance-based > Hierarchical > BIRCH
❑ BIRCH (Balanced Iterative Reducing and Clustering Using Hierarchies)
▪ Procedure
• Two parameters
‒ Branching factor: maximum number of children
‒ Threshold: maximum diameter of sub-clusters stored at the leaf nodes
1. CF-Tree building (i.e., low-level micro-clustering)
‒ For each object in the dataset, find the closest leaf entry, add the object to the leaf entry, and update the CF 
‒ If the leaf node is full, split it into two leaf nodes and add one more entry in the parent
2. Global clustering (i.e., high-level macro-clustering)
‒ Applying a standard clustering method (e.g., k-means) on the leaf nodes of the CF tree 
▪ Issue
• Sensitive to insertion order of data points
• Since we fix the size of leaf nodes, clusters may not be so natural
• Clusters tend to be spherical given the diameter measures

❑ Motivation
▪ Most partitioning and hierarchical methods are designed to find spherical-shaped clusters
▪ What if we want to find arbitrarily-shaped clusters

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Density-based
❑ Density-based clustering
▪ Clusters are formed as dense regions in the data space, separated by sparse regions
▪ Major features
• Discover clusters of arbitrary shape
• Robust to noise
• Single-scan of datasets (only examine the local region to estimate density)
• No need for the predefined number of clusters
• Need density parameters for density estimation and termination condition
▪ Methods
• DBSCAN (connected region-based density)
• DENCLUE (density estimation function)
• CLIQUE (grid-based density approximation)

❑ DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise)
▪ How can we find dense (and sparse) regions? 
→ The density of an object can be measured by the number of other objects close to it

COSE471: Data Science

Clustering > Density-based > DBSCAN
❑ DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise)
▪ A density-based notion of cluster as a maximal set of density-connected points
▪ Main parameters
• Eps(ε): maximum radius of the neighborhood
‒ Eps-neighborhood of a point x: NEps(x) = {p | d(p, x) ≤ Eps, p!=x}
• MinPts: minimum number of points in the Eps-neighborhood of a point

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Density-based > DBSCAN
❑ DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise)
▪ A density-based notion of cluster as a maximal set of density-connected points
▪ Main parameters
• Eps(ε): maximum radius of the neighborhood
‒ Eps-neighborhood of a point x: NEps(x) = {p | d(p, x) ≤ Eps, p!=x}
• MinPts: minimum number of points in the Eps-neighborhood of a point
▪ Types of points
• Core point: in a dense neighborhood (i.e., cluster)
‒ i.e., |NEps(x)| ≥ MinPts
• Border point: not a core point, but the neighbor of a core point
‒ i.e., |NEps(x)| < MinPts, but x ∈ NEps(x’) for a core point x’
• Outlier/noise: neither a core point nor the neighbor of a core point

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Density-based > DBSCAN
❑ DBSCAN
▪ A density-based notion of cluster as a maximal set of density-connected points
▪ Reachability and Connectivity
• Directly density-reachable
‒ A point p is directly density-reachable from a point q, if p is in the neighborhood of a core point q
‒ i.e., p ∈ NEps(q) and |NEps(q)| ≥ MinPts
• Density-reachable 
‒ A point p is density-reachable from a point q, if there is a chain of points where consecutive 
points are directly density-reachable
‒ i.e., For p1(=q),…, pi-1, pi, pi+1,…, pn(=p), pi+1 is directly density-reachable from pi
• Density-connected
‒ A point p is density-connected to a point q, if there is a point o such that both p and q are 
density-reachable from o
▪ [Recap] a density-based cluster = a maximal set of density-connected points
• i.e., every point is density-reachable from any point within the set

Clustering > Density-based > DBSCAN
❑ Discussion
▪ Complexity: O(n2) or O(nlogn) if spatial index is used
▪ Advantages
• Does not need to know the number of clusters
• Can find arbitrarily shaped clusters
• Has a notion of noise – robust to outliers
▪ Disadvantages
• Hard to determine the proper parameter values (Eps and MinPts)
• Ineffective to data sets with large density difference
‒ Example

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Density-based > DBSCAN
❑ Heuristics for determining Eps and MinPts
▪ Main idea
• For points in a cluster, their k-th nearest neighbors are at closer distance
• For noise points, their k-th nearest neighbor at farther distance
▪ MinPts: a rule of thumb
• E.g., 2*dim = 4 for two-dimensional data or ln(n) for n points
▪ Eps: the first valley of the sorted k(=MinPts)-dist graph 
• The slope of the curve becomes noticeably more horizontal (i.e., the elbow method)
• k-dist(p): return the distance from a point p to its k-th nearest neighbor
• Sorted k-dist graph: sorting the points by their k-dist values

COSE471: Data Science

Clustering > Probabilistic
❑ Motivation
▪ Traditional clustering
• Assign each data point exclusively to one cluster with clear boundaries between clusters
• i.e., hard clustering
▪ Probabilistic clustering 
• Assign each data object over multiple clusters with the probability of it belonging to each cluster
• i.e., soft clustering
70

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Probabilistic
❑ Motivation
▪ Traditional clustering
• Assign each data point exclusively to one cluster with clear boundaries between clusters
• i.e., hard clustering
▪ Probabilistic clustering 
• Assign each data object over multiple clusters with the probability of it belonging to each cluster
• i.e., soft clustering

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Probabilistic
❑ Idea
▪ A probabilistic cluster is a distribution over the data space 
• Can be represented as a probability density function
▪ A set of observed objects is a mixture of instances from 
multiple probabilistic clusters
• Assume that each observed object is generated independently
▪ Infer a set of k probabilistic clusters that are mostly likely 
to generate the data set
72Image: https://towardsdatascience.com/gaussian-mixture-model-clearly-explained-115010f7d4cf
 
❑ Motivation
▪ Assign each data object over multiple clusters with the 
probability of it belonging to each cluster

Clustering > Probabilistic
❑ Probabilistic model-based clustering
▪ A set C of k probabilistic clusters c1, …,ck with probability density functions (PDF) f1, …, fk, 
respectively, and their weights w1, …, wk
▪ Probability of an object o generated by cluster cj is
𝑃 𝑜 𝑐𝑗 = 𝑤𝑗𝑓𝑗 𝑜   
▪ Probability of an object o generated by the set of clusters C = {c1, …, ck} is
𝑃 𝑜 𝐶 = σ𝑗=1
𝑘 𝑤𝑗𝑓𝑗(𝑜) 
▪ Since objects are assumed to be generated independently, for a data set D = {o1, …, on},
𝑃 𝐷 𝐶 = ς𝑖=1
𝑛 𝑃 𝑜𝑖 𝐶 = ς𝑖=1
𝑛 σ𝑗=1
𝑘 𝑤𝑗𝑓𝑗 𝑜𝑖  
❑ How to find a set C of k probabilistic clusters such that P(D|C) is maximized?
▪ Maximizing P(D|C) is often intractable since the PDF of a cluster can take an arbitrary form
▪ To make it computationally feasible, assume the PDFs are some parameterized distributions

COSE471: Data Science

Clustering > Probabilistic > EM
❑ Expectation-Maximization 
▪ An iterative method to find the maximum likelihood of parameters in statistical models, where the 
model depends on unobserved latent variables
▪ Two repeated main steps
• Expectation step: computes the expected likelihood using the current estimate for the parameters
• Maximization step: computes parameters maximizing the expected likelihood found on the E step
→ Repeat the E-M steps until the parameters converge
▪ Example
• In the context of clustering
‒ Expectation: assign each object to the cluster with a center that is closest to the object
‒ Maximization: adjust the centers so that the similarity of objects in a cluster to its center is maximized
→ Repeat the E-M steps until the clustering results converge
• Anything come to mind?
75
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Probabilistic > EM
❑ Computing probabilistic mixture models with EM
▪ Given n objects 𝐷 =  {𝑥1, … , 𝑥𝑛}, find a set of parameters 𝛩 = 𝜃1, … , 𝜃𝑘  to maximize 𝑃(𝐷|𝛩)
• e.g., 𝜃𝑗  =  (𝜇𝑗, σ𝑗) are the mean and standard deviation of the j-th univariate Gaussian distribution 
▪ Initially assign random values to 𝜃𝑗, then iteratively conduct the E/M steps until convergence

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Evaluation
❑ “Clusters are in the eye of the beholder”
▪ For (supervised) classification, we have a variety of measures to evaluate how good our model is
• e.g., accuracy, precision, recall, F1
▪ For (unsupervised) clustering analysis, how can we evaluate the “goodness” of the clusters?
❑ Major issues in clustering analysis
▪ Clustering tendency
• Assess the suitability of clustering - any inherent grouping structure?
▪ The number of clusters
• Determine the right number of clusters for a given data set and algorithm
▪ Clustering quality
• Evaluate the quality of the clustering results in extrinsic or intrinsic ways
81
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Evaluation > Clustering Tendency  
❑ Clustering tendency (i.e., clusterability)
▪ Evaluate whether the dataset has any “inherent grouping structure”
• Non-random structure that may lead to meaningful clusters
▪ Measures
• Spatial histogram (qualitative)
‒ Contrast the histogram of the data with that generated from random samples  
• Distribution distance (quantitative)
‒ Compare the empirical probability mass function from the data with those 
from the randomly generated samples
‒ e.g., Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence
• Hopkins statistic
‒ A statistic for the spatial randomness of a variable as distributed in a space. 
‒ Given a d-dimensional space S and a data set D in S, 
𝑥𝑖 = distance from a randomly sampled data in S to its nearest neighbor in D
𝑦𝑖 = distance from a randomly sampled data in D to its nearest neighbor in D
82
Image: https://complex-systems-ai.com/en/data-partitioning/hopkins-statistic/
𝐻 = σ𝑖=1
𝑛 𝑥𝑖

𝑛 𝑥𝑖
𝑑 + σ𝑖=1
𝑛 𝑦𝑖
𝑑
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Evaluation > Number of Clusters
❑ The number of clusters controls the proper granularity of cluster analysis
▪ Finding a good balance between compressibility and accuracy in cluster analysis
• Depending on the distribution's shape and scale in the data set
• Depending on the clustering resolution required by the user
▪ Two undesirable extremes
• The whole data set is one cluster: no value of clustering → Each point as a cluster: no data summarization
❑ Methods for determining the number of clusters k
▪ Empirical approach
• Rule of thumb: 𝑘 ≈ 𝑛/2 for a dataset of n points (e.g., n = 200 → k = 10)
‒ Each cluster is expected to have about 2𝑛 points
• Elbow method: the turning point in the curve of the cluster variance with k
‒ The cluster variance: the sum of squared distances of data to its centroid, a.k.a. inertia
▪ Statistical approach
• Find the optimal number of clusters that results the best statistics
• e.g., Dunn index, Silhouette coefficient, etc.
83Image: https://ankitajhumu.medium.com/selecting-number-of-clusters-in-k-mean-clustering-d60a1f85d65b/

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Evaluation > Clustering Quality 
❑ Unsupervised measure (i.e., intrinsic index)
▪ Examine how compact clusters are and how well clusters are separated with distance metrics
▪ Measures
• Dunn index
• Silhouette coefficient
❑ Supervised measure (i.e., extrinsic index)
▪ Examine the extent to which cluster labels match externally given ground truth cluster labels
▪ Measures
• Information-based: Normalized mutual information (NMI)
• Pairwise comparison-based: Jaccard index, Rand index
84
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Evaluation > Clustering Quality > Dunn Index
❑ Unsupervised measure (i.e., intrinsic index)
▪ Criteria
• Cluster cohesion: how closely related are objects in a cluster?
• Cluster separation: how distinct a cluster is from other clusters?
▪ Dunn index (extreme situations)
• The intra-cluster compactness Δ = max𝐶 𝑜𝑖 =𝐶(𝑜𝑗) 𝑑 𝑜𝑖, 𝑜𝑗
‒ The maximum distance between two points that belong to the same cluster 
• The inter-cluster separation 𝛿 = min𝐶 𝑜𝑖 ≠𝐶(𝑜𝑗) 𝑑 𝑜𝑖, 𝑜𝑗
‒ The minimum distance between two points that belong to different clusters
• The Dunn index 𝐷𝐼 =
𝛿
Δ
‒ The larger the ratio, the farther away the clusters are separated comparing 
to their compactness
• Using the extreme distances can be affected by outliers

Clustering > Evaluation > Clustering Quality > Comparison-based 
❑ Supervised measure (i.e., extrinsic index)
▪ Dataset D = {o1, …, on}, Ground truth G = {G1, …, Gl}, Clustering result C = {C1, …, Cm}, 
▪ Pairwise comparison-based
• Treat each cluster in the ground truth as a class
‒ For each pair of objects (oi, oj) in D, 
 if they are assigned to the same cluster, the assignment is regarded as positive; otherwise, negative 
‒ Depending on assignments, we have four possible cases for the total number of pairs (i.e., 𝑛
2 ) 
• Basic metrics
‒ Jaccard index = TP/(TP + FP + FN) 
‒ Rand index = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN)
• Cf. advanced metrics: adjusted rand index (ARI), B-cubed score
89Image: wikipedia

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Clustering > Evaluation > Clustering Quality > Comparison-based 
❑ Example
▪ Dataset D = {a, b, c, d, e}
▪ Ground truth G = [G1={a,b,c}, G2={d,e}]
▪ Clustering result C = [C1= {a,b}, C2 = {c,d,e}] 
▪ All possible pairs  = 5
2 = 10 
• (a,b),(a,c),(a,d),(a,e),(b,c),(b,d),(b,e),(c,d),(c,e),(d,e)
▪ Counting each case
• TP = 2: (a,b), (d,e)
• FP = 2: (c,d), (c,e)
• FN = 2: (a,c), (b,c)
• TN = 4: (a,d), (a,e), (b,d), (b,e)
▪ Rand index = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN) = 2 + 4 / (2 + 2 + 2 + 4) = 0.6
90
